title: Linear Function Tables: Find the Rule Behind the Rows

scenes.title: Is this table really linear?
body: The y-jumps are +6 and +12 — so why can this still be linear?
scenes.narration: Look at a table with the points one comma five, four comma eleven, and ten comma twenty-three. The y-values do not increase by the same amount, so is the table still linear? Here is the idea: linear does not mean equal y-jumps by themselves. It means a constant rate of change — the same change in y for each one unit of change in x.

scenes.title: Compare rates, not raw jumps
scenes.narration: The first x-gap is three while the first y-gap is six, so the rate is six over three, or two. The second x-gap is six and the y-gap is twelve, so the rate is twelve over six, also two. Notice why this works: the second input change is twice as large, and the output change is twice as large too. The ratio stays the same.

scenes.title: The common table mistake
body: Wrong test: compare only consecutive y-differences
Correct test: compare Δy / Δx over matching rows
scenes.substitution: unequal x-gaps can still produce one constant slope
scenes.narration: This is where students often mix things up. Equal y-differences prove a constant rate only when the x-differences are equal too. If the x-gaps change, you must divide. A table is linear when the output changes proportionally to the input change, which is exactly what slope measures.

scenes.title: Turn the table into an equation
body: Use one row to find b in y = mx + b
scenes.narration: Once we know the slope is two, the whole table follows one straight-line rule. Use the point one comma five in y equals m x plus b. Five equals two times one plus b, so b equals three. The equation is y equals two x plus three. The two records the constant rate, and the three is the output the rule would have when x is zero.

scenes.title: Quick verification
body: A linear table is one constant-rate rule written in rows.
scenes.narration: Quick check: put x equals ten into y equals two x plus three. We get twenty-three, exactly the table value. So do not ask whether the y-values jump by the same amount. Ask whether change in y divided by change in x stays constant. That constant ratio is the slope, and it is what makes the table linear. The full lesson is available on SUMMIT.
